title: The neuroprotective effect of statin in traumatic brain injury: A systematic review

sections.abstract: Despite recent encouraging pharmaceutical and technical breakthroughs in neurosurgical critical care, traumatic brain injury (TBI)-related mortality and morbidity remain substantial clinical issues. Medication of statins was revealed to enhance outcomes following TBI in animal research. In addition to their main role of decreasing serum cholesterol, statins decrease inflammation and enhance cerebral blood flow. However, research on the efficacy of statins in TBI is still limited. This systematic review was conducted to determine the efficacy of statins in enhancing the clinical outcomes of TBI individuals, and specifically investigate the optimal dose and form of statins. The databases of PubMed, DOAJ, EBSCO, and Cochrane were extensively researched. The date of publication within the last fifteen years was the inclusion criterion. Meta-analyses, clinical trials, and randomized controlled trials were prioritized forms of research publications. Ambiguous remarks, irrelevant correlations to the main issue, or a focus on disorders other than TBI were the exclusion criteria. Thirteen research were included in this study. Simvastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin were the main form of statins discussed in this study. Enhancement of the Glasgow Coma Scale, survival rates, hospital length of stay, and cognitive outcomes were revealed in this study. This study suggests either simvastatin 40 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, or rosuvastatin 20 mg for 10 days as the optimal therapeutic forms and doses to be applied in the management of TBI. Pre-TBI statin use was linked to lower risk of mortality in TBI individuals compared to nonusers, whereas statin discontinuation was linked to an increase in mortality.
sections.introduction:
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is considered to impact sixty-nine million people annually worldwide. Among all trauma-related injuries, TBI continues to be the main cause of mortality and disability, with serious medical, family, social, and economic impacts. 1 Despite recent encouraging pharmaceutical and technical breakthroughs in neurosurgical critical care, TBI-related mortality and morbidity are still high and a substantial clinical problem. 2 To ameliorate the outcomes of TBI, no entirely efficacious pharmacotherapies have been developed. 3

The most essential managements for TBI individuals are currently supportive measures, direct monitoring, and surgical management, but therapeutic outcomes are still dismal. As a result, more efficacious therapy choices for these individuals are urgently needed to promote and enhance therapeutic outcomes. 4 The Operation Brain Trauma Therapy (OBTT) consortium was founded to identify potential pharmacotherapies for TBI in both the short and long term, from animal research to clinical trials in humans. The consortium has proposed statins as a feasible medication for TBI and its sequelae due to their properties of minimizing neuroinflammation and enhancing cerebral blood flow (CBF) following a TBI. 5

Medication of statins or 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitors was revealed to enhance outcomes after TBI in animal research. 6 , 7 , 8 In addition to their main role of decreasing serum cholesterol, statins decrease inflammation and enhance CBF. 9 In preclinical investigations, statins diminish injury-related brain edema, oxidative stress, amyloid protein aggregation, and neuroinflammation. Statins also decrease the generation of inflammatory cytokines and promote the integrity of the blood–brain barrier (BBB). 7 , 10 , 11 , 12 This systematic review was conducted to determine the efficacy of statins in enhancing the clinical outcomes of TBI individuals, and specifically investigate the optimal dose and form of statins.
sections.methods:
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) protocols were employed in this systematic review. The Individual, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) framework was also used to develop eligibility criteria. Table 1 shows the PICO criteria. Table 1 PICO formulation. Table 1 Patient/Problem (P) Intervention (I) Comparison (C) Outcome (C) Traumatic brain injury Statin Standard therapy Improvement of Glasgow Coma Scale, survival rate, hospital length of stay and cognitive outcome Type of Clinical Question Intervention Study Design Meta-analyses, clinical trials, and randomized controlled trials

PICO formulation.

The databases of PubMed, DOAJ, EBSCO, and Cochrane were extensively researched. To conduct more inquiries, the following keywords were employed.: “efficacy” or “HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor” or “statin” or “traumatic” or “brain” or “injury”. The date of publication within the last fifteen years was the inclusion criterion.

According to the PRISMA statement, the titles and abstracts of the records that were gathered were checked, and the entire texts of those that were judged relevant were examined. Meta-analyses, clinical trials, and randomized controlled trials were prioritized forms of full-text research articles; thus, a total of sixteen research were selected. In the end, twelve research were included in this systematic review. While the other four articles were eliminated due to similarity to other articles, ambiguous remarks, irrelevant correlations to the main issue, or a focus on disorders other than TBI. Fig. 1 shows the PRISMA flow diagram for the research identification and selection process, whereas Table 2 shows the list of articles that made up the systematic review. In clinical management, statin use should not be discontinued after TBI. Khokhar et al 5 2018 Mortality and Associated Morbidities Following Traumatic Brain Injury in Older Medicare Statin Users Retrospective cohort study 100.515 ✓ When appropriate, atorvastatin and simvastatin can be considered to older adults with TBI in order to decrease mortality and associated morbidities. Lokhandwala et al 6 2020 Preinjury Statins Are Associated With Improved Survival in Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury Retrospective study 270 ✓ Preinjury statin use in isolated traumatic brain injury patients is associated with improved outcomes. Sanchez-Aguilar et al 7 2013 Effect of rosuvastatin on cytokines after traumatic head injury Randomized controlled trial 36 ✓ Statins may induce an anti-inflammatory effect and may promote recovery after TBI. Khokhar et al 9 2017 In-Hospital Mortality Following Traumatic Brain Injury Among Older Medicare Beneficiaries, Comparing Statin Users With Nonusers Retrospective study 112.109 ✓ Current use of atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, and simvastatin was associated with a significant decrease in in-hospital mortality following TBI among older adults. Redelmeier et al 10 2019 Association Between Statin Use and Risk of Dementia After a Concussion Cohort study 28.815 ✓ Older adults had a substantial long-term risk of dementia after a concussion, which was associated with a modest reduction among 9.patients receiving a statin. Farzanegan et al 11 2017 Effects of atorvastatin on brain contusion volume and functional outcome of patients with moderate and severe traumatic brain injury; a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial Randomized controlled trial 44 ✓ Even though atorvastatin was not found to be more effective than placebo in reducing contusion expansion rate, it was associated with improved functional outcomes at 3-months following moderate to severe TBI. Tapia-Perez et al 12 2008 Effect of rosuvastatin on amnesia and disorientation after traumatic brain injury (NCT003229758) Randomized controlled trial 21 ✓ Statins may reduce amnesia time after TBI, possibly by immunomodulation. It remains to be seen whether statin discontinuation is a proxy variable for injury severity, or whether it exerts deleterious effects after injury. Orlando et al 14 2013 Unintentional discontinuation of statins may increase mortality after traumatic brain injury in elderly patients: a preliminary observation Cohort study 61 ✓ Unintended discontinuation of statin therapy is associated with increased mortality in the elderly TBI population. Continuing in-hospital statin therapy in PIS users may be an important factor in the prevention of in-hospital mortality in this elderly TBI population. sections.results:
We discovered a total of 125 research using the initial search method. Because of the non-relevant title, 34 articles were eliminated. There were 91 articles left with a relevant title. We eliminated 75 articles based on title and abstract screening. Experimental animal research and literature review articles were excluded. We eventually have thirteen articles included in this systematic review after screening and qualitative evaluation. Simvastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin were the main form of statins discussed in all research. All authors of the journals included in this systematic review stated that they had no conflicts of interest to disclose.

The effect of oral simvastatin 40 mg daily for 10 days in individuals with TBI was researched by Shafiee et al, revealing that administration of simvastatin had a substantial impact in enhancing Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score in severe TBI individuals. Either simvastatin or placebo was given via nasogastric tube. At the time of admission, no substantial statistical difference was reported between the simvastatin and control groups in terms of mean GCS score. At discharge, the simvastatin group had 18.9% conscious individuals, while the control group had just 3.1%. The proportion of conscious individuals in the simvastatin group increased substantially (64.9%) compared to the control group one month after discharge (28.1%). On the day of discharge and one month following release, nevertheless, individuals who took simvastatin had a mean GCS score that was greater than that of the controls. In terms of mortality rate and length of mechanical ventilation (MV), intensive care unit (ICU), and neurosurgery ward stay, there were no substantial differences between the two groups. Although, individuals receiving simvastatin had lower mortality rates, and lower duration of MV, ICU, and neurosurgical wards, compared to the control group. Furthermore, no notable adverse effects were documented in this research. 2

Farzanegan et al researched the effect of oral atorvastatin 20 mg daily for 10 days on brain contusion volume and functional outcome in individuals with moderate-to-severe brain injuries. At 3 months after injury, the functional outcome scales of the Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS), Modified Rankin Scale (MRS), and Disability Rating Scale (DRS) were better, though atorvastatin was not revealed to be better than placebo in decreasing the rate and volume of contusion expansion. 11 In individuals with moderate-to-severe TBI, Soltani et al found that taking oral atorvastatin 20 mg daily for 10 days enhanced GCS and DRS levels in 2–3 months after the research and enhanced GOS from the tenth day after the research in individuals with moderate-to-severe TBI. No adverse effects were reported in this research. 4 The medication was given to each individual within 10 h of the accident in both research. 4 , 11

The effect of oral rosuvastatin 20 mg daily for 10 days on cytokines after TBI was researched by Sanchez-Aguilar et al and demonstrated a substantial impact of rosuvastatin on reducing tumor necrosis factor-α levels. The levels of interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, and IL-10 did not appear to be affected by rosuvastatin administration. Statins might induce anti-inflammatory effects and be linked to a decrease in disability scores following a TBI, indicating a favorable functional outcome. 7 Another research by Tapia-Perez et al researched the effect of oral rosuvastatin 20 mg daily for 10 days on amnesia and disorientation after TBI, suggesting statins might diminish amnesia time after TBI with a hazard ratio of 53.76, possibly by immunomodulation. 12 Patients admitted to the emergency room who were stable and fulfilled the inclusion criteria were randomly assigned to receive either oral rosuvastatin or placebo immediately. In the context of a skull base fracture, a nasogastric or orogastric catheter was inserted in case of swallowing worsened. There were no life-threatening adverse effects identified in both research. 7 , 12

Redelmeier et al explored the correlation between statin use and the incidence of post-concussion dementia, revealing that individuals who used statins within 90 days immediately following a concussion had a 13% lower risk of dementia than those who did not take statins. Atorvastatin, cerivastatin, fluvastatin, lovastatin, pitavastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, and simvastatin were among the statins investigated. The usage of rosuvastatin was linked to the greatest risk reduction, whereas simvastatin was linked to the smallest. Lipophilic statins were slightly more efficacious than hydrophilic statins. Higher dosages did not provide a better benefit than lower ones. Those who started taking statins after the concussion had a substantial risk decrease, but those who stopped taking statins after the trauma had no meaningful risk reduction. Otherwise, no patients were ruled out. 10

Khokhar et al investigated the link between post-TBI statin use and mortality, as well as the occurrence of related morbidities, revealing that any form of statin use was linked with decreased 30-day, 60-day, and 90-day death after discharge from TBI. Statin use in any form was linked to a lower risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes, incident depression, and ADRD (Alzheimer's disease and related dementias). Atorvastatin and simvastatin, in particular, were linked to substantial reductions in all TBI sequelae outcomes. 5 While another previous research also by Khokhar et al comparing statin pre-TBI users and nonusers, found that current usage of atorvastatin, simvastatin, and rosuvastatin was linked to a substantial reduction in the risk of in-hospital death following TBI. Pre-TBI statin usage was defined as more than 30-day period prior to TBI. All three statins lowered 30-day mortality considerably, whereas rosuvastatin and simvastatin lowered 60-day mortality substantially. 9

Research about the pre-TBI administration of statins was conducted by Lokhandwala et al and revealed that individuals using statins had a decreased in-hospital mortality rate (11% versus 21%), skilled nursing facility disposition (19% versus 28%), and a higher median GOS-extended (11 [9–13] versus 9 [8–10]) compared to those who were not. In terms of hospital length of stay (LOS) and critical care unit LOS, no differences were discovered between the two groups. 6 Schneider et al researched the association between pre-TBI statin use survival and functional recovery in older moderate to severe TBI individuals, revealed that statin usage was related to a 76% reduced adjusted risk of in-hospital death, 76.7% of those discharged alive survived 1 year, and 66.8% had full GOS-extended. At three months, statin users and nonusers had the same risk of excellent recovery. Statin users had a 13% greater chance of excellent recovery 12 months after injury. 15 In their meta-analysis, Mu et al revealed that pre-TBI statin use was linked to a lower risk of mortality in TBI individuals compared to nonusers.

Orlando et al looked at the impacts of discontinuing statins on mortality in an older adult population with TBI and found no evidence of a substantial increase in in-hospital mortality following pre-TBI statin discontinuation compared to statin continuation. 13 Even though their earlier research on the impacts of in-hospital statin discontinuation on individual outcomes in older TBI individuals found that those who discontinued taking statins had a 4-fold greater mortality rate than those who continued. Statin discontinuation did not result in a greater complication rate when compared to statin continuation, and there was no difference in the proportion of individuals who spent more than one week in the hospital. 14 In both research, pre-TBI statin patients who were not given an in-hospital statin within 48 h after admission were deemed to have stopped taking statins, whereas pre-TBI statin patients who got in-hospital medications included the delivery of a statin during the first 48 h after admission were deemed to be on statin treatment. 13 , 14 In their meta-analysis, Mu et al also emphasized statin discontinuation was linked to an increase in mortality. 3
sections.discussion:
The treatment of TBI has evolved over the last decades, with a greater emphasis on preventing and treating secondary injuries. Secondary injury is the series of cellular, neurochemical, and metabolic changes brought on by the primary insult and which persist over time. Biochemical changes, inflammation, swelling, and ischemic processes cause multiple secondary injuries, including intracellular accumulation of potassium and calcium, neuroinflammation, free radical damage, and excitotoxicity, as well as oxidative stress and apoptosis, all of which contribute to the severity of primary brain injury and secondary hemorrhage. In turn, local hypoxia and ischemia, herniation, and eventual neuronal cell death via necrosis and apoptosis may result from the increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) that results from the BBB breaking down and the development of edema. 4 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 Many TBI survivors may experience short- and long-term disability and consequences as a result of their injuries, putting tremendous clinical, social, and economic stress on the healthcare system and society. 2

Central nervous system injury is still the leading cause of death following trauma, preceded by exsanguination, sepsis, and multi-organ failure, according to a recent assessment of the epidemiology of civilian trauma deaths. There has been a decline in the proportion of deaths owing to hemorrhages, contrary to deaths from TBI, sepsis, and multi-organ failure, which have not diminished over the previous ten years. These illnesses are closely linked to harmful inflammation that is both excessive and persistent. 24 , 25

TBI sequelae might appear days, months, or years after the initial injury due to chronic neuroinflammation following injury, in addition to a surge in mortality in the elderly. This persistent inflammatory cascade has been linked to various negative outcomes, including stroke, depression, and ADRD. 5 Limiting neuroinflammation after a brain injury can theoretically lead to lower mortality and morbidity, supporting the intriguing potential value of anti-inflammatory medicines in the treatment of TBI individuals. 2

Although the exact pathophysiological process of TBI is unknown, neuroinflammation has been identified as a possible primary mechanism. Following a TBI, the release of a large number of cytokines and chemokines causes an initial inflammatory reaction in the central nervous system, which can aggravate the damage caused by the TBI. 2 Statins have been demonstrated in research employing animal models and different cell types to offer defense against a variety of assaults, including N-methyl- d -aspartate (NMDA) and glutamate, amyloid beta-protein, oxygen-glucose deprivation, sodium nitroprusside, and bone morphogenetic protein. 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 Statins have been demonstrated to diminish thrombosis, subsequent vascular injury, and lesion volume after TBI. 16 , 34 Statins may have neuroprotective effects, such as preserving CBF, which decreases the risk of Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, and age-related cognitive decline. 10 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 Additionally, after TBI, there has been observed a neuroprotective impact on neurons in the cornu ammonis area 3 (CA3) region, leading to a notable enhancement in spatial learning at later time points. The delay in cognitive enhancement observed in these trials raises the hypothesis that statins may affect apoptosis. This theory is backed by the later finding that simvastatin-treated animals have a considerably lower ratio of Bax/Bcl-2, which favors an antiapoptotic state. 16 , 32 , 41 Statins have been also revealed to enhance neurogenesis, decrease apoptosis, lower microglial activity, and thereby minimize inflammation-induced astroglial activation. 2 , 20 , 42 , 43 These findings imply that statins, regardless of systemic cholesterol levels, may contribute to microvascular homeostasis and immunological regulation. 10 The neuroprotective and neurorestorative character of statins is a result of a variety of interactions. Some of these effects are mediated at the level of the microvasculature, such as their capacity to increase nitric oxide bioavailability, which controls cerebral perfusion and enhances endothelial function, and their capacity to stabilize atherosclerotic plaques; others are mediated outside of this system, such as the capacity of statins to act as antioxidants, anti-inflammatory agents, immunomodulatory substances, and regulators of progenitor cells. 16 , 44 Fig. 2 shows the statin effects in TBI. 1 Fig. 2 Statin effects in Preinjury, Acute, Subacute and Chronic Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI). GOS = Glasgow Outcome Scale; Bax/Bcl-2 = Bcl-2 associated X protein; BBB = blood brain barrier; BNDF = brain-derived neurotrophic factor; eNOS = endothelial isoform of nitric oxide synthase; PKB = protein kinase B; PI3K = phosphoinositide-3-kinase; VEGF = vascular endothelial growth factor; VEGFR2 = vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2; vWF = von Willebrand Factor. Fig. 2

Statin effects in Preinjury, Acute, Subacute and Chronic Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI). GOS = Glasgow Outcome Scale; Bax/Bcl-2 = Bcl-2 associated X protein; BBB = blood brain barrier; BNDF = brain-derived neurotrophic factor; eNOS = endothelial isoform of nitric oxide synthase; PKB = protein kinase B; PI3K = phosphoinositide-3-kinase; VEGF = vascular endothelial growth factor; VEGFR2 = vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2; vWF = von Willebrand Factor.

It has also been proposed that the neuroprotective benefits of statins may be partially caused by a decrease in farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) and/or geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) levels, which decreases the number of prenylated proteins and may or may not be independent of cholesterol. FPP and GGPP, two isoprenoids upstream of cholesterol in that pathway, are gaining more attention for both their normal functions and their potential roles in the pathophysiology of ischemic heart disease, malignancy, and neurodegenerative diseases. FPP and GGPP are isoprenoids, along with other compounds like ubiquinone and dolichol. FPP, a C15 isoprenoid, is a crucial branch point in the synthesis of cholesterol, ubiquinone, dolichol, and GGPP. In addition to playing an essential role in protein synthesis, FPP prenylated small GTPases like H-ras, Rheb, and other proteins that include cysteine in the C-terminal CaaX box (C = cysteine, a = aliphatic amino acid, and X = C-terminal amino acid) posttranslationally. FPP is a substrate for the enzyme geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase, which produces GGPP instead of FPP, which has 15 carbons instead of GGPP's 20. GGPP, on the other hand, prenylated proteins with a C-terminal leucine residue, such as the Rac-1 and Rho family of GTPases, in contrast to FPP, which prenylated proteins with cystine in the CaaX box of the C terminal. These and other prenylated proteins regulate a variety of cellular processes, including intracellular vesicle transport, cell adhesion, endocytosis, cytoskeletal architecture, receptor signaling, cell cycle progression, and gene expression. They are essential parts of complex signaling networks. 8

Mountney et al researched the potential beneficial efficacy of simvastatin in a model of severe penetrating TBI using an intravenous route of administration. Simvastatin was administered intravenously at 30 min and 6 h after frontal penetrating ballistic-like brain injury (PBBI) and continued once daily for either 4 or 10 days after PBBI in rats. Rotarod testing found severe motor deficits across the board in all damage groups, but no discernible therapeutic advantages from simvastatin. The Morris water maze (MWM) test revealed cognitive impairment in all PBBI-damaged mice; however, a 10-day simvastatin therapy reduced these effects. Animals dramatically enhanced their scores for latency to platform and retention, whereas the 4-day treatment regimen had no discernible effect. Simvastatin significantly decreased glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), IL-1, and IL-17 serum levels by 4.0, 2.6, and 7.0-fold, respectively, after 4 h following injury, according to biomarker and cytokine analyses. 45

Lu et al investigated the efficacy of statins (simvastatin and atorvastatin) on spatial learning and neurogenesis in rats that had undergone controlled cortical impact (CCI). Atorvastatin and simvastatin were administered to rats daily for 14 days beginning the day after TBI. The study revealed that statin treatment of TBI enhances spatial learning on days 31–35 after TBI, decreases neuronal loss after TBI in the non-neurogenic region of the hippocampal CA3 region, enhances neurogenesis in the neurogenic region of the dentate gyrus, and enhances TBI–induced angiogenesis. At the same dose, simvastatin medication is revealed more effective therapeutically than atorvastatin treatment. 41

In another CCI mouse model of TBI, Chauhan and Gatto investigated whether the combined effects of cell proliferative property of erythropoietin and the neuroregenerative property of simvastatin would result in maximum recovery. Results demonstrated that simvastatin was more efficacious than erythropoietin in repairing axonal damage after TBI while simvastatin was more successful than erythropoietin in increasing cell proliferation compared to baseline TBI. Simvastatin and erythropoietin therapy together maximally restored axonal integrity while also causing more proliferation of newly generated cells, leading to a superior functional recovery after TBI than either therapy used alone. 46

Indraswari et al describe the optimal statin and dose regimen in murine of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and TBI to promote translation to clinical practice. Simvastatin, rosuvastatin, and vehicle were given to mice in a preclinical model of TBI at doses of 1 mg/kg and 5 mg/kg for 5 days following the impact. The highest enhancement in functional outcomes after TBI was shown with the dose of rosuvastatin 1 mg/kg. Treatment with rosuvastatin was linked to histological evidence of lessened neuronal degeneration at 24 h after TBI, lessened microgliosis at 7 days after TBI, and retained neuronal density in the CA3 region at 35 days after the injury. The downregulation of inflammatory gene expression in the brain was also linked to the administration of rosuvastatin after TBI. Following ICH, simvastatin 1 mg/kg therapy was linked to the largest enhancement in functional outcomes; this benefit was unaffected by the extent of the hemorrhage. 47

Peng et al researched the benefit of statins on cognitive deficits in adult male rodents after TBI and revealed that statins have statistically substantial favorable impacts on cognitive function following TBI, according to the meta-analysis. According to the stratified analysis, simvastatin and atorvastatin had the highest impacts on memory retention and acquisition, respectively, although statin impacts on memory acquisition are greater in models with closed head injury. Further meta-regression analysis revealed that animal type, research quality, and anesthetic agent all affected how well statins affected memory retention. Their systematic review concluded that statins may diminish cognitive deficits following TBI. 48

In managing various neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, ischemic stroke, and TBI, statins are generating a lot of interest, notwithstanding some debate. 8 An HMG-like component in all statins interacts with 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase. The degree of HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is indicated by statin potency. Because of its property to make numerous polar interactions with the HMG-CoA reductase enzyme, rosuvastatin is the most potent. The next most potent statin is atorvastatin, which is preceded by simvastatin, fluvastatin, and pravastatin. Because of their polar groups, pravastatin and rosuvastatin are hydrophilic, whereas lovastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin, and simvastatin are lipophilic. Lipophilic medications diffuse more easily through cell membranes, making them more easily absorbed into tissues where they can alter intracellular processes or cause toxicity. In comparison to the remaining statins (which have a half-life of 3 h), rosuvastatin and atorvastatin have a longer half-life (20 and 14 h, respectively). 1

When using statins to treat TBI, there may be a threshold where the pharmacological impacts of statins become more apparent. Shafiee et al stated that the administration of oral simvastatin 40 mg had a substantial impact in enhancing GCS on the day of discharge and one-month following release. 2 Farzanegan et al and Soltani et mentioned that oral atorvastatin 20 mg substantially enhanced GOS, MRS, and DRS in moderate-to-severe brain injury individuals, whereas other research by Sanchez-Aguilar et al and Tapia-Perez et al noted that oral rosuvastatin 20 mg might induce immunomodulation and be linked to a decrease in disability scores following a TBI. 7 , 4 , 11 , 12 Oral administration of statin was the preferred route of drug administration in all studies, however, a nasogastric or orogastric catheter was inserted in case of swallowing worsening in the context of a skull base fracture or severe TBI. 2 , 7 , 12 All five studies concluded that 10-day period was the optimal period for statin medication post-TBI.

Two studies by Sanchez-Aguilar et al and Tapia-Perez et al started the statin medication immediately after the patients were resuscitated, while the other two studies by Farzanegan et al and Soltani et al started the medication to each individual within 10 h of the accident. 4 , 7 , 11 , 12 Furthermore, two studies by Orlando et al emphasized to start continuing pre-TBI statin in patients who got in-hospital medications within 48 h after admission. 13 , 14

In their meta-analysis, Mu et al demonstrated that pre-TBI statin use was linked to a lower risk of mortality in TBI individuals compared to nonusers. 3 Lokhandwala et al revealed that pre-TBI usage of statins had a decreased in-hospital mortality rate, skilled nursing facility disposition, and a higher median GOS-extended. 6 Schneider et al researched the association between pre-TBI statin use survival and functional recovery in older moderate to severe TBI individuals, revealed that statin usage was related to a 76% reduced adjusted risk of in-hospital death, 76.7% of those discharged alive survived 1 year, and 66.8% had full GOS-extended, additionally, statin users had a 13% greater chance of excellent recovery 12 months after injury. 15 However, no period of pre-TBI statin usage was specified in those three research. 3 , 6 , 15 Another previous research by Khokhar et al emphasized that pre-TBI statin usage was defined as more than 30-day period prior to TBI. 9

One study by Redelmeier et al revealed that individuals who used statins within 90 days immediately following a concussion had a 13% lower risk of dementia than those who did not take statins. Rosuvastatin use was linked to a greater risk decrease in post-concussion dementia, whereas simvastatin use was linked to the least risk reduction. Higher dosages did not provide a better benefit than lower ones. 10 Khokhar et al emphasized that continuing any form of statin use post-TBI was linked with decreased 30-day, 60-day, and 90-day death after discharge from TBI. Post-TBI usage of statin in any form was linked to a lower risk of stroke, depression, and ADRD. Atorvastatin and simvastatin, in particular, were linked to substantial reductions in all TBI sequelae outcomes. 5 Comparing statin pre-TBI users and nonusers, another previous research by Khokhar et al also found that current usage of atorvastatin, simvastatin, and rosuvastatin was linked to a substantial decline in the risk of in-hospital death following TBI. All three statins lowered 30-day mortality considerably, whereas rosuvastatin and simvastatin lowered 60-day mortality substantially. 9 Mu et al emphasized statin withdrawal was associated with an increase in mortality. 3 In older TBI individuals, Orlando et al found no evidence that discontinuing pre-injury statin following TBI would significantly increase in-hospital mortality as compared to continuing statin, even though their past studies discovered that those who discontinued taking statins had a 4-fold higher mortality risk than those who continued. 13 , 14

In an outindividual context, statin therapy for hypercholesterolemia has been proven to have few adverse effects, the most frequent adverse effects include myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, hepatotoxicity, and diabetic mellitus. With rates ranging from 1 to 10% of patients, myalgia is the most frequent adverse reaction to statin therapy. The likelihood of developing myopathy is dose-dependent and can manifest as diffuse myalgias or as other unexplained muscle pain or weakening, which will go away when the medication is stopped. The most severe adverse effect of statin use is rhabdomyolysis, which is exceedingly uncommon (less than 0.1%), with a spike in creatine kinase higher than 10 times the upper limit of normal and concomitant symptoms such as myoglobinuria, renal impairment, and changes in serum electrolytes. In as many as 1%–3% of patients taking statin therapy, increased hepatic transaminases have been reported. This normally dose-dependently happens within the first three months of starting medication, and it is not typically linked to chronic hepatic impairment. This rise is typically a temporary response that goes away with continuing therapy or shortly after an interruption in therapy. In addition to disrupting insulin signaling pathways, statins have been demonstrated to alter pancreatic beta cell function, raise insulin resistance, and increase the risk of diabetes mellitus. It is unclear whether trauma individuals or individuals with hypoperfusion are more likely to experience this issue. Therefore, the risk that statins could exacerbate acute traumatic coagulopathy needs to be taken into account. Decreased tissue factor activity, thrombin production, thrombin activity, decreased fibrinogen levels, and changes in tissue plasminogen activator and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) activity are all statin-related effects on hemostasis. Additionally, statins have been revealed to decrease platelet activity. However, statins have not been linked to clinically substantial coagulopathy in trauma individuals, according to reports. The risk of malignancy, dementia, mood disorders, interstitial lung disease, and acute interstitial nephritis is not increased by statins, according to research. 24 , 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 , 56

Statins are contraindicated for individuals with active hepatic disease or unexplained chronic aminotransferase increases. Statins are now generally considered contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding due to their impact on the cholesterol pathway, which is required for fetal and infant steroid synthesis and cell membrane development. The use of statins and fibrates combination for mixed dyslipidemia is related to a 5% higher risk of myopathy. Coadministration of simvastatin and gemfibrozil is also not recommended due to the risk of rhabdomyolysis. Grapefruit juice is a cytochrome p450 3A4 inhibitor that can enhance the risk of toxicity when used with atorvastatin, lovastatin, and simvastatin. Coadministration of CYP3A4 substrate statins (atorvastatin, lovastatin, and simvastatin) with potent 3A4 inhibitors (diltiazem, erythromycin, and -azoles) may result in higher serum concentrations and an increased risk of adverse effects. Anti-epileptic medicines like phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbitone are strong inducers of cytochrome p450 enzymes and may be linked to lower statin drug levels. 24 , 49 , 50 , 57 , 58 , 59 , 60 , 61

Fortunately, no life-threatening adverse effects were reported in all research included in this systematic review. All the probable adverse effects and contraindications were considered as the exclusion criteria of the studies. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 15 , 13 , 14

Recent studies indicate that statin therapy substantially reduces cardiovascular disease-related morbidity and mortality while also substantially enhancing or curing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) in humans. However, research on the efficacy of statins in TBI is still limited. 62 Most studies in this systematic review are limited by sample sizes and methodological differences, such as varying forms and doses. Further large-scale studies are required to conclude the optimal form and therapeutic dose and period of statins in the management of TBI.

sections.conclusion: The majority of research revealed that statins provided substantial neuroprotective effects in TBI individuals. Enhancement of the Glasgow Coma Scale, survival rates, hospital length of stay, and cognitive outcomes were revealed in the research . This research also suggests either simvastatin 40 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, or rosuvastatin 20 mg for 10 days as the optimal forms and doses to be applied in the management of TBI. Pre-TBI statin use was linked to a lower risk of mortality in TBI individuals compared to nonusers, whereas statin discontinuation was linked to an increase in mortality. Further large-scale studies are required to conclude the optimal form and therapeutic dose and period of statins in treating TBI.
